label: Figure 12.1: A natural monopoly
alt: A steeply declining LRAC curve for a piped-water network, with the full-market demand curve D1 and AR1 lying above LRAC between q1 and q2, while the halved demand curve D2 and AR2 that each of two firms would face lies below LRAC everywhere.
caption: The long-run average cost curve LRAC for a piped-water network declines steeply as fixed network costs are spread over more customers — a classic natural monopoly. A single firm facing the whole market’s demand, D<sub>1</sub> & AR<sub>1</sub>, can earn abnormal profit at any output between q<sub>1</sub> and q<sub>2</sub>, since AR<sub>1</sub> lies above LRAC across that range. If a second firm entered and industry demand were split in two, each firm would face the smaller D<sub>2</sub> & AR<sub>2</sub> curve, which lies below LRAC at every output — neither could even cover its costs. The market can profitably support only one supplier.
